title: High-Precision Homomorphic ALU over Arbitrary Moduli with $O(1)$ Bootstrapping
authors: Jiaming Liu, Shihe Ma, Anyu Wang, and Xiaoyun Wang
abstract:
Homomorphic computation on large integers requires both arithmetic and non-arithmetic (e.g., Boolean) operations.
The radix-based method by Cha et al. (EUROCRYPT'26) supports both operation types over arbitrary $n$-bit integers with a complexity of \(O(\log n)\) and \(O(1)\) bootstrapping, respectively.
Meanwhile, the triangle encoding method by Gao and Zheng (CRYPTO'26) has a complexity of \(O(1)\) bootstrapping in arithmetic mode, but is restricted to power-of-two integers.
Its arithmetic-to-Boolean (A2B) conversions also needs \(O(n)\) bootstrapping and is only \(O(1)\) in the amortized sense. 

This work improves both methods by supporting computation over arbitrary moduli with \(O(1)\) bootstrapping for both operation types, and is a generalization of Gao and Zheng's approach.

Our first contribution is a framework for efficient homomorphic arithmetic over arbitrary plaintext moduli.
It supports flexible radix representations and uses a CVP-based method to find defining polynomials with well-conditioned canonical embeddings and small norm growth under ring operations.
When the method fails to find suitable defining polynomials, we use homomorphic Montgomery multiplication over radix-friendly plaintext rings, where each Montgomery reduction requires only $O(1)$ bootstrapping calls. 
Our second contribution is an efficient arithmetic-to-digit (A2D) conversion using $O(1)$ bootstrapping calls, independent of the radix used by the arithmetic representation.

We implemented our method in OpenFHE.
For P-384 and Curve25519, our arithmetic multiplication achieves $8.67\sim10.26\times$ and $12.57\sim13.41\times$ lower latency than CPL26's LazyMult and ExactMult, respectively.
The speedups increase to $17.47\sim27.24\times$ and $25.35\sim35.63\times$ in the amortized setting.
For RSA-1024 and RSA-2048, our arbitrary-modulus multiplication achieves $4.25\times$ and $7.58\times$ lower latency and $16.74\times$ and $29.85\times$ lower amortized time than CPL26's ExactMult, respectively.
For 64-, 128-, and 256-bit messages, our A2B conversion is $3.75\times$, $6.40\times$, and $14.17\times$ faster than GZ26, respectively.

      arithmetic and non-arithmetic (e.g., Boolean) operations. The radix-based

      over arbitrary n-bit integers with a complexity of O(log n) and O(1)

      to-Boolean (A2B) conversions also needs O(n) bootstrapping and is only

      plaintext rings, where each Montgomery reduction requires only O(1)

1   Introduction

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted
data and provides a powerful foundation for privacy-preserving computation [22].


                                           1
Over the past decade, several families of FHE schemes have been developed,
each optimized for a particular computation model. For example, BGV and BFV
provide exact SIMD arithmetic over finite plaintext rings [12,19], CKKS supports
approximate SIMD arithmetic over complex numbers [15], while FHEW and
TFHE are designed for Boolean computation with fast bootstrapping [18,16].
    Despite this diversity, existing FHE schemes remain highly specialized and
do not yet provide an efficient counterpart of the general-purpose computation
readily available on plaintext data. Three limitations are particularly relevant
to integer computation. First, high-precision computation is expensive, because
increasing the precision typically leads to faster noise growth, larger parameters,
and more costly bootstrapping [16,14]. Second, arithmetic and non-arithmetic
operations are usually efficient in different ciphertext representations. Supporting
both within the same computation therefore often requires costly conversions
between arithmetic-friendly and Boolean-friendly ciphertexts [10,27,30,26]. Third,
the choice of plaintext modulus is often constrained by the underlying scheme.
For instance, BGV/BFV achieve their best SIMD packing efficiency only for
a small class of plaintext primes, whereas FHEW/TFHE mostly operate with
power-of-two plaintext moduli. Consequently, simultaneously supporting high
precision, mixed arithmetic and non-arithmetic computation, and arbitrary integer
moduli remains challenging.
    A substantial amount of work has explored high-precision SIMD homomor-
phic computation. In the direction of BGV/BFV, GBFV [21], dBFV [29], and
REFHE [11] extend BFV-style encoding to efficiently support high-precision
integer computation with slow noise growth. In another direction, discrete CKKS
stores integers within CKKS slots and serves as the foundation for high-precision
integer arithmetic [17,4,5]. Building on this framework, several recent works
have pushed the supported precision substantially further and extended the
computation model.
    Boneh and Kim decompose large integers into small residue numbers before
encoding them into discrete CKKS ciphertexts, enabling homomorphic compu-
tation on integers with thousands of bits [7]. Kim takes a different approach
of representing integers modulo B k with their radix-B digits [23,24]. Because
arithmetic causes the underlying digit representation to grow in both size and
length, CKKS bootstrapping is used to reduce it back to a (relaxed) small-norm
representation. The original construction requires O(k log k) bootstrappings per
ciphertext multiplication, which is later reduced to O(log k). Cha et al. [13]
further improved this radix-based approach by introducing a faster bootstrapping
procedure that restores either a relaxed or exact small-norm representation using
O(log k) bootstrappings. They also extend the construction to arbitrary plaintext
moduli through homomorphic Montgomery reduction.
    More recently, Gao and Zheng propose the triangle encoding, a combination
of discrete-CKKS with the REFHE representation. They simulate arithmetic in
Z[X]/(X k − X + 2, X − 2) within CKKS slots, thereby realizing SIMD arithmetic
over Z2k [20]. Their construction supports both arithmetic and Boolean operations:

    Among these discrete-CKKS-based constructions, the radix-based method
of Cha et al. and the triangle encoding method of Gao and Zheng represent
two complementary state-of-the-art approaches to high-precision homomorphic
integer computation. The former supports arbitrary plaintext moduli and needs
only a constant number of bootstrappings for non-arithmetic operations, but
requires O(log k) bootstrappings for arithmetic operations. The latter achieves
O(1) bootstrapping in arithmetic operations, but is restricted to power-of-two
moduli and requires O(k) bootstrappings for A2B conversion. Therefore, no
existing construction simultaneously provides high-precision computation over
arbitrary integer moduli and constant-complexity support for both arithmetic
and non-arithmetic operations.
    This raises the following question:
       Can we support high-precision computation over arbitrary integer
      moduli, with O(1) bootstrapings for both arithmetic and non-arithmetic
                                   operations?
    We answer this question affirmatively. Table 1 compares our method with
existing works.

1.1    Our Contributions
Our work makes the following contributions.

 – FHE for arbitrary integer moduli. We introduce a polynomial represen-
   tation for modular integer computation together with a CVP-based method
   for finding suitable defining polynomials. It supports leveled SIMD arithmetic
   with one CKKS level per multiplication, and admits arithmetic bootstrapping
   that refreshes approximation error and polynomial overflow separately or
   jointly. For moduli without a suitable defining polynomial, we utilize homo-
   morphic Montgomery reduction for efficient computation. By expressing the


                                          3
   digit reduction as linear transformations of the arithmetic representation,
   we avoid the radix carry procedure required by CPL26 and obtain arbitrary
   modulus multiplication with only O(1) bootstrap calls.
 – Faster ALU with O(1) bootstrapping. We give arithmetic-to-digit con-
   version using exactly two functional bootstrap calls and logarithmic multi-
   plicative depth, together with a digit-to-arithmetic conversion requiring only
   linear operations. The arithmetic-to-Boolean conversion can be realized in the
   same number of bootstrap calls and multiplicative depth. For M = 2n , the
   same construction directly outputs the bits of the integer, giving arithmetic-
   to-Boolean conversion with two functional bootstrap calls and enabling a
   SIMD ALU that combines arithmetic and Boolean computation.
 – Implementation and evaluation. We implement our constructions in
   OpenFHE and evaluate them across different integer moduli and arithmetic
   bases. For P-384 and Curve25519, our arithmetic multiplication achieves
   up to 10.26×/13.41× lower latency and 27.24×/35.63× lower amortized
   cost than CPL26’s LazyMult/ExactMult. For RSA-1024 and RSA-2048, our
   arbitrary-modulus multiplication achieves 4.25×/7.58× lower latency and
   16.74×/29.85× lower amortized cost than CPL26’s ExactMult. Our A2B
   conversion is 3.75×, 6.40×, and 14.17× faster than GZ26 for 64-, 128-, and
   256-bit messages, respectively.

Bootstrapping arithmetic ciphertexts. Homomorphic arithmetic increases
both the overflow polynomial and the CKKS approximation error, which can
be refreshed separately or together. The overflow refresh does not eliminate the
overflow polynomial, but replaces it with a new bounded one. We multiply by
(X − b)−1 to separate the integer overflow from the message, reduce the resulting
integer part modulo a small modulus, and use modulus raising to return to the
arithmetic representation with bounded overflow. The approximation error can be
refreshed separately by isolating the error, bootstrapping it, and subtracting the
result from the original ciphertext, leaving the same arithmetic polynomial with
a smaller error. When both refreshes are required, we fuse the two procedures so
that they share the linear transformations.

1.3   Organization
Section 2 reviews the FHE and CKKS tools used in our construction. Section 3
introduces the arithmetic polynomial representation, CKKS packing, homomor-
phic arithmetic, and the defining-polynomial search procedure. Section 4 presents
overflow refresh, error refresh, complete arithmetic bootstrapping, and multipli-
cation over arbitrary moduli. Section 5 introduces the digit representation and
conversions between arithmetic and digit representations, including arithmetic-to-
Boolean conversion as a special case and its extension to general integer moduli.
Section 6 reports our implementation and experimental evaluation. Appendix A
gives the detailed proofs, Appendix B gives the defining-polynomial search and
example constructions, and Appendix C gives the detailed conversion algorithm
and analysis.

7   Conclusion

We presented a framework for efficient SIMD homomorphic integer computation
over arbitrary plaintext moduli. Our arithmetic polynomial representation sup-
ports leveled addition and multiplication with one CKKS level per multiplication,
together with arithmetic refresh for controlling approximation error and poly-
nomial overflow. For moduli admitting suitable defining polynomials, we give
a CVP-based method for finding such polynomials, while general moduli are
handled through homomorphic Montgomery multiplication over fixed arithmetic
spaces using only O(1) bootstrap calls.
    We further presented an arithmetic-to-digit conversion that supports differ-
ent arithmetic bases and output radices. The conversion uses O(1) functional
bootstrap calls and logarithmic-depth carry computation, and directly yields
arithmetic-to-Boolean conversion as a special case. Together, these techniques
provide efficient arithmetic, representation conversion, and non-arithmetic com-
putation within a unified SIMD framework.

C.2   Cost of General Arithmetic-to-Digit Conversion
The conversion uses exactly two functional bootstrap calls. The second bootstrap
returns |Λ|(|C|2 + |C|(1 + hκ )) ciphertexts corresponding to the carry indicators,
the candidate checks, and the radix-b digits of each candidate κ.
    Each of the ⌈log2 ℓ⌉ carry-composition levels uses |Λ||C|2 rotations, 2|Λ||C|2
ciphertext–plaintext multiplications, and |Λ||C|3 ciphertext–ciphertext multipli-
cations. All products within one composition level are independent, so the carry
computation has multiplicative depth ⌈log2 ℓ⌉.
    Combining the final-carry indicators with the candidate checks and the digits
of κ adds one multiplicative level. The prefix products over Λ require ⌈log2 |Λ|⌉
levels, and forming and applying the exclusive selectors adds two further levels.
All remaining rotations and digit reconstruction are linear, so the multiplicative
depth followingPthe second bootstrap is at most ⌈log2 ℓ⌉+⌈log2 |Λ|⌉+3. The prefix
products use δ∈{1,2,4,...}, δ<|Λ| (|Λ| − δ) ciphertext–ciphertext multiplications,
and forming the exclusive selectors uses another |Λ| − 1. The final selection
uses |Λ|(1 + hκ ) ciphertext–ciphertext multiplications. The same operations act
simultaneously on all occupied intervals in a SIMD batch.
